report.source_text: Accordingly, intravenous ganciclovir treatment (5 mg per kg per day over two weeks) was initiated. Over the following three weeks, serum PCR for CMV turned negative. Tetraparesis slowly improved, with still moderate pareses of the upper (between MRC 3 and 4), but severe pareses of the lower (between MRC 1 and 2) extremities at neurological reassessment four weeks after symptom onset. Unfortunately, in the further course the patient developed a septic syndrome, most likely owing to a pulmonary focus, and exspired due to septic multiple organ failure. Autopsy was prohibited.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 51-year-old immunocompromised patient, six weeks post-stem cell transplant for myelodysplastic syndrome, developed high-grade pure motor flaccid tetraparesis and an acute confusional state. Brain MRI revealed new symmetrical subcortical hyperintensities in the precentral gyrus. CSF analysis showed a normal cell count, slightly elevated protein and albumin, but was negative for CMV and other viral PCRs. However, serum CMV PCR showed a progressively increasing viral load (up to 8,600 copies/ml) starting shortly prior to the development of tetraparesis. Intravenous ganciclovir treatment was initiated, leading to serum CMV PCR turning negative and slow improvement of the tetraparesis. The patient later developed septic syndrome and expired due to septic multiple organ failure.

CSF PCR was negative for CMV and other common neurotropic viruses (HSV 1/2, VZV, EBV, HHV6, JC virus, adenovirus, enterovirus, poliovirus) and bacterial DNA.

Tetraparesis slowly improved after ganciclovir treatment, with moderate pareses of the upper and severe pareses of the lower extremities at neurological reassessment four weeks after symptom onset.
Patient later developed septic syndrome and expired due to septic multiple organ failure.
